stem: A 68-year-old man is brought to the hospital due to 2 days of progressive shortness of breath and cough. He has a history of severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and has had multiple recent exacerbations and several hospitalizations over the past year. During his last hospitalization, he had acute respiratory failure requiring endotracheal intubation. This prompted the patient to make a living will specifying that he does not want any resuscitative measures or invasive therapies in the event of a life-threatening emergency. On examination, he is lethargic and arousable only to noxious physical stimuli. His temperature is 37.2 C (99 F), blood pressure is 132/70 mm Hg, pulse is 102/min, and respirations are 32/min. Examination reveals diffusely decreased breath sounds, bilateral expiratory wheezes, and labored breathing. It is determined that he lacks decision-making capacity. His daughter says, "I have been taking care of my father for many years and I know him better than anyone. He would not want any aggressive measures. Please just make him comfortable." However, the patient's wife demands that everything be done to save her husband's life, including intubation if necessary. She insists that she knows what her husband would have wanted and threatens to file a lawsuit. Which of the following interventions is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Consult the hospital ethics committee
options.B: Meet with all family members to achieve consensus on a course of action
options.C: Obtain a court order to proceed with intubation
options.D: Proceed with endotracheal intubation if medically indicated
options.E: Respect the patient's living will and provide comfort care only

explanations.A: Initiating a family meeting would be the first step if the family members disagreed about the course of action and there was no living will and/or no designated health care proxy in place. Referral to the hospital ethics committee or the courts for a judgment would become necessary if no consensus was achieved.
explanations.B: Initiating a family meeting would be the first step if the family members disagreed about the course of action and there was no living will and/or no designated health care proxy in place. Referral to the hospital ethics committee or the courts for a judgment would become necessary if no consensus was achieved.
explanations.C: Initiating a family meeting would be the first step if the family members disagreed about the course of action and there was no living will and/or no designated health care proxy in place. Referral to the hospital ethics committee or the courts for a judgment would become necessary if no consensus was achieved.
explanations.D: Proceeding with CPR or intubation would violate the patient's wishes as expressed in his living will.

generalExplanation: A living will (advanced directive) specifies a patient's wishes for health care in advance of losing the ability to communicate or of becoming incapable of making his or her own decisions. In this case, the patient is incapacitated and his family members strongly disagree on the best course of action; both claim to have a better understanding of what the patient would have wanted in the current situation. However, the physician's responsibility is to the patient, and ethically the physician must adhere to the patient's wishes as outlined in the living will. The living will protects the patient's autonomy and overrules the wishes of any family members.
educationalObjective: A living will communicates the patient's own wishes if he or she becomes incapacitated, and it overrules the wishes of the family.

stem: A 34-year-old man is admitted to the hospital due to recurrent pancreatitis following a 2-week period of heavy alcohol consumption. He has a long history of alcohol abuse and has been through inpatient alcohol treatment programs on multiple occasions. The patient realizes he needs to stop, but says he drinks when he is home alone and feels stressed. Medical history is notable for hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus, treated with lisinopril and metformin. Blood pressure is 146/85 mm Hg and pulse is 72/min. BMI is 46 kg/m². On examination, the patient appears comfortable. Fasting glucose is 183 mg/dL and hemoglobin A1c is 8.2%. The patient says he is not willing to return to an inpatient alcohol treatment program after hospital discharge but might consider outpatient counseling. Which of the following is the most appropriate response to this patient?

options.A: I am concerned that you do not understand how alcohol affects your diabetes.
options.B: I really think that going back to inpatient alcohol treatment is in your best interest.
options.C: If you don't take your alcoholism more seriously, one day it will kill you.
options.D: Let's schedule an appointment with an outpatient program that can see you as soon as possible.
options.E: Tell me some ways that outpatient alcohol treatment might help you.
options.F: Whenever you are ready to be serious about your problems, I will be here to help you.

explanations.A: Abasic discussion of disease processes and complications can provide motivation for change and is most appropriate for a patient in the precontemplation stage. However, this patient acknowledges that change is needed and is willing to consider at least some treatment options. Continued emphasis on consequences from lack of change is likely only to promote anxiety and frustration.
explanations.C: Abasic discussion of disease processes and complications can provide motivation for change and is most appropriate for a patient in the precontemplation stage. However, this patient acknowledges that change is needed and is willing to consider at least some treatment options. Continued emphasis on consequences from lack of change is likely only to promote anxiety and frustration.
explanations.B: These statements do not acknowledge patient autonomy. Even if the physician is certain that inpatient treatment would benefit the patient, a better understanding of the patient's perspective is needed before pushing him to do what he does not want. Making arrangements to schedule an appointment with a treatment program before the patient is agreeable may diminish his commitment to treatment. Such actions are more appropriate for a patient in a preparation stage who can collaborate with the physician and take some responsibility for treatment.
explanations.D: These statements do not acknowledge patient autonomy. Even if the physician is certain that inpatient treatment would benefit the patient, a better understanding of the patient's perspective is needed before pushing him to do what he does not want. Making arrangements to schedule an appointment with a treatment program before the patient is agreeable may diminish his commitment to treatment. Such actions are more appropriate for a patient in a preparation stage who can collaborate with the physician and take some responsibility for treatment.
explanations.F: It is important to convey to all patients, in all stages of change, that their physician is committed to their benefit and is willing to help. However, this patient's willingness to consider treatment options shows that he takes his condition seriously, and this statement would likely be seen as condescending.

generalExplanation:
The psychotherapeutic technique of motivational interviewing is used to encourage patients to change maladaptive behaviors. Interventions are geared to the patient's stage of readiness to change. Elements include a nonjudgmental stance focusing on the patient's intrinsic motivation to change, acknowledging ambivalence and resistance to change, and supporting the patient's autonomy and efforts to take responsibility.

This patient has recurrent alcoholic pancreatitis and has failed previous attempts at inpatient alcohol rehabilitation, but he is willing to consider outpatient therapy (contemplation stage). Appropriate steps at this point would be to explain how referral for outpatient treatment might work, discuss the pros and cons of outpatient treatment compared to inpatient treatment, and assess the patient's conviction (understanding of the importance of change) and confidence (self- perceived ability to change). The physician should allow the patient time to consider all options and should also arrange follow-up for planning the next steps in treatment.

stem: An 84-year-old man with end-stage progressive idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, who has received home hospice care for 4 months, suddenly begins refusing food. The patient had previously tolerated regular food and fluid intake, which his family provides daily. His symptoms of respiratory distress and pain are managed with palliative medications but have worsened significantly over the past 2 weeks. The patient is emaciated and bedbound. The patient tells the hospice nurse and the physician that he wants to "go on a fast" and expresses his desire to avoid all food and liquid. He states, "I know this means I could die sooner, but I have lived a full life. I can feel that my time is near, and I am at peace." The patient's family expresses grief and emotional distress after hearing his request. The patient is alert and fully oriented without evidence of cognitive impairment. Which of the following is the most appropriate next action?

options.A: Arrange an ethics consultation to determine whether the patient's request can be honored
options.B: Counsel the patient on potential consequences and record his preferences for comfort measures
options.C: Counsel the patient that his request cannot be honored because it is intended to hasten death
options.D: Counsel the patient that his request cannot be honored because it violates the principle of beneficence
options.E: Withhold oral intake but administer intravenous fluids if the patient develops clinical dehydration

explanations.A: Ethics consultation is not necessary because this patient has no evidence of cognitive impairment and is receiving hospice care, with advanced illness and poor prognosis.
explanations.C: Although VSED is likely to hasten death, it generally falls within the purview of patient autonomy and does not differ in principle from other patient refusals (eg, Do Not Resuscitate order).
explanations.D: The principle of beneficence requires a physician to act in the patient's interest to relieve suffering but does not supersede a competent patient's informed decision and autonomy to choose VSED.
explanations.E: In most cases, management of thirst symptoms with intravenous fluids is not recommended because it does not improve patient comfort or reduce delirium severity.

generalExplanation:
Goals of patient care (eg, hospice care) in terminal illness include preserving patient autonomy and prioritizing patient comfort. Patients with terminal illness may voluntarily cease fluid and food intake (ie, voluntarily stopping of eating and drinking [VSED]) to signal a symbolic readiness for death. Although VSED can potentially increase a patient's physical suffering and may hasten death, it can also increase psychological comfort by promoting autonomy over the dying process. When a patient requests VSED, the physician should proceed as follows:

• Confirm that the patient is cognitively intact and that the request for VSED is voluntary and not influenced by mental illness « Counsel the patient (and family members) regarding possible consequences, including severe thirst and associated discomfort e Discuss alternatives to VSED (eg, continuing fluids only, decreasing rather than eliminating oral intake) e Discuss and clearly record the patient's preferences for managing discomfort (eg, small sips of fluids, oral swabbing, ice chips) because delirium and cognitive impairment may occur
educationalObjective: Voluntarily Stopping of Eating and Drinking is a decision by patients with terminal illness to cease all food and fluid intake, often as a symbolic acceptance of death. Physicians should verify that the patient has decision-making capacity and is acting voluntarily, provide counseling regarding potential consequences (eg, discomfort), and record preferences for comfort (eg, oral swabbing) in case of thirst-induced cognitive impairment (eg, delirium).

stem: A 29-year-old primigravida at 36 weeks gestation comes to the office with her husband for a routine prenatal visit. Her pregnancy has been uncomplicated, and she has no chronic medical conditions. Her only medication is a daily prenatal vitamin. Vital signs are normal. Fundal height is 36 cm, and fetal heart sounds are 150/min on Doppler ultrasound. The patient says she has created a detailed birth plan and would like to have a natural delivery. She says a vaginal birth is necessary for her to feel fully connected to her baby, and she is not interested in receiving any medication to decrease the pain. The patient's wishes are acknowledged and documented in the chart; however, the physician states that unexpected events can occur during labor and delivery that require a cesarean delivery. The patient replies, "A cesarean delivery is not part of my birth plan—t don't want to have one." Which of the following is the most appropriate response?

options.A: "Birth plans are good for uncomplicated deliveries, but in an emergency, you can trust that my recommendation is the safest option."
options.B: "I don't feel comfortable not being able to perform a cesarean delivery in an emergency. I can refer you to another provider if you would like."
options.C: "I would only recommend a cesarean delivery if it were absolutely necessary. Let's talk about what the indications would be."
options.D: "If you do not want a cesarean delivery, I will not perform one. I will make sure to document this in your chart."
options.E: "My priority is to take care of you and your baby, so if the baby is in distress during labor, I will need to do a cesarean delivery."

explanations.A: These responses are paternalistic, dismissing the patient's request and asking her to trust the physician without conducting an informed consent discussion. Instead, the patient should be empowered to make a fully informed decision by being educated about risks and benefits of vaginal versus cesarean delivery in specific situations.
explanations.E: These responses are paternalistic, dismissing the patient's request and asking her to trust the physician without conducting an informed consent discussion. Instead, the patient should be empowered to make a fully informed decision by being educated about risks and benefits of vaginal versus cesarean delivery in specific situations.
explanations.B: It would be premature to refer the patient to another provider or to merely document the patient's decision without first discussing the indications for cesarean delivery and addressing the patient's specific reservations. The physician may be able to resolve the patient's concerns so there is agreement about when a cesarean delivery is necessary.
explanations.D: It would be premature to refer the patient to another provider or to merely document the patient's decision without first discussing the indications for cesarean delivery and addressing the patient's specific reservations. The physician may be able to resolve the patient's concerns so there is agreement about when a cesarean delivery is necessary.

generalExplanation:
Although this patient has expressed her wishes for a vaginal delivery, it is the physician's duty to inform her that unexpected complications can occur in normal pregnancies that may necessitate a cesarean delivery to protect both her and her fetus. By conducting a thorough informed consent discussion in advance (an example of preventive ethics), the physician has the opportunity to explain the indications for an emergency cesarean delivery and review the risks and benefits in an unhurried, unpressured atmosphere.

Routine prenatal care visits present an ideal setting in which to initiate discussion of potential pregnancy complications and prevent future misunderstanding and disagreement. The informed consent process should include a clear description of the specific circumstances in which cesarean section would be indicated, as well as a general overview of cesarean section as the patient gets closer to delivery. The physician can then directly address the patient's specific reservations about cesarean delivery and take time to answer any questions she may have.

stem: A 48-year-old woman is admitted to the oncology service for the 4th time in 2 months. She was diagnosed with breast cancer 2 years ago and has endured surgery, chemotherapy, and radiation. She also participated in multiple experimental trials. Unfortunately, her disease has progressed. Today, the patient is hospitalized for hemoptysis and shortness of breath. She complains of severe pain in her back and has lost another 5 pounds since she was discharged 2 weeks ago. Her body mass index is 17 kg/m². The patient has expressed a wish to stop all treatment, go home, and enjoy her remaining days. She is found to have the capacity to make this decision. The oncologist, patient, and patient's family decide that hospice care is the most appropriate plan. Which of the following is considered a requirement for referring a patient for hospice care?

options.A: Greater than 75% decline in ability to complete activities of daily living
options.B: Lack of family or other caregivers to assist the patient
options.C: Patient has a do not resuscitate order
options.D: Patient has a prognosis of <6 months
options.E: Patient has decision-making capacity

explanations.A: Although functional decline is involved in assessing prognosis, it is not a required criterion for hospice eligibility.
explanations.B: Lack of family and caregiver assistance is not a requirement. In fact, many hospice services are designed to provide support for families and caregivers.
explanations.E: Patients should be included in all decisions as long as they have capacity. In those lacking capacity, decisions regarding hospice care can be made using advanced planning directives or surrogate decision makers.

generalExplanation:
Hospice services provide interdisciplinary palliative care for patients with a prognosis of <6 months. Hospice care involves a patient-centered approach that emphasizes quality of life, comfort, and death with dignity. It is appropriate when aggressive curative treatments are no longer beneficial or desired. The physician must substantiate a prognosis of <6 months with documentation of irreversible decline in clinical and functional status.

Hospice services include comfort measures (eg, control of pain and dyspnea), logistical support (eg, home health care, durable medical equipment), psychological and spiritual counseling, and bereavement support. Hospice services can be provided in a home, nursing home, assisted living facility, or dedicated facility.

Common misunderstandings regarding hospice eligibility include beliefs that the patient must be actively dying and have a do not resuscitate order (Choices C and F). While most patients on hospice care have clear instructions to decline heroic life-sustaining measures, this is not a prerequisite to receive hospice services.
educationalObjective: Hospice is a palliative, interdisciplinary model of care for patients with a prognosis of <6 months. The focus is on symptom control; quality of life; and psychosocial, spiritual, and bereavement care.

stem: A 73-year-old woman comes to the emergency department due to shortness of breath and productive cough for the past 2 weeks. The patient lives independently and is active in her retirement community. She was seen by her primary care physician last year and has no medical conditions. The patient has a history of smoking but quit 20 years ago. Temperature is 37.8 C (100 F). Lung auscultation reveals right-sided crackles. Chest x-ray reveals right lower lobe consolidation and a solitary 1-cm, round lesion in the left upper lung field, which was not seen on previous x-rays. The patient is admitted and treated for community-acquired pneumonia, becomes medically stable, and is ready to be discharged home with oral antibiotics. The physician records the pulmonary lesion finding on the discharge summary, places an outpatient radiology referral for chest CT scan, and informs the patient that she will be contacted regarding her radiology appointment after discharge. Several months later, the patient is readmitted to the hospital with dyspnea and weight loss. Records show that she was called about the scheduled appointment for the CT scan but did not attend it, so the test was not completed. Repeat imaging reveals enlargement of the pulmonary nodule, and biopsy confirms lung adenocarcinoma. Which of the following interventions by hospital providers is most appropriate for reducing future occurrences of similar errors?

options.A: Explaining the importance of primary care follow-up after discharge
options.B: Informing patients' family members about follow-up imaging studies
options.C: Monitoring results from pending appointments for all discharged patients
options.D: Postponing discharge until imaging studies and biopsy results are complete

explanations.B: Including family members in follow-up care is useful if the patient has cognitive impairment or has consented to sharing medical information with them. However, for independent, cognitively intact patients (eg, this woman), direct engagement through counseling is preferred for building awareness and promoting follow-up.
explanations.C: Monitoring results from pending appointments on all discharged patients extends beyond hospital providers' scope of responsibility (eg, inpatient management of acute health concerns) and potentially compromises patient safety by excessively increasing provider workload. Primary care providers often receive a log of their patients' abnormal outpatient tests through the electronic medical record, enabling superior systematic monitoring and follow-up.
explanations.D: Postponing discharge of medically stable patients until completion of nonurgent studies and biopsy results, which may take several extra days, is not recommended because it increases nosocomial infection risk and undermines resource stewardship (eg, use of efficient health care resources).

generalExplanation:
Fewer than 20% of inpatients with incidentally detected lung nodules undergo recommended postdischarge follow-up (eg, CT scan, management based on malignancy risk), leading to preventable adverse outcomes, including delayed cancer diagnoses. Acommon cause is loss to follow-up after transfers of care (eg, hospital discharge), as seen in this patient. Because inpatient care focuses on acute medical conditions, patients may not recognize the importance of assessing unrelated findings (eg, incidental lung or adrenal nodule) after discharge, especially when symptoms resolve. Timely (<4 weeks) primary care follow-up promotes completion of pending studies (eg, imaging, laboratory tests) and health management (eg, new medications, diagnoses). During the discharge process, patients should receive high-quality provider communication and counseling explaining the importance of follow-up, as this increases patient likelihood of attending primary care visits and completing follow-up recommendations. High-quality communication includes the following: e Face-to-face discourse, allowing responses to nonverbal cues e Patient-centered interaction tailored to the patient's current motivations, goals, and ability e Interactive approaches for verifying patient understanding (eg, inviting questions, encouraging teach-back that summarizes patient understanding of the conversation)

Discharge summaries can be routed to primary care providers for review when patients attend their posthospitalization appointment.

stem: A 62-year-old woman with a history of multiple medical conditions, including coronary artery disease, hypertension, and osteoarthritis, arrives by ambulance at the emergency department after tripping and falling down the stairs. The patient is currently on vacation with friends and new to the hospital system, with no history available in the electronic medical record. Blood pressure is 170/105 mm Hg and pulse is 75/min. She is alert, fully oriented and conversant, but in severe pain. X- ray reveals a fracture of the right hip necessitating emergency surgical repair. As the patient is admitted to the hospital, the nurse prepares to create a list of the patient's home medications in the electronic medical record. Of the following practices, which is likely most effective in reducing errors related to medication reconciliation during this patient's hospitalization?

options.A: Calling the patient's family first to obtain a list of home medications
options.B: Obtaining a medication record from the patient's pharmacy only
options.C: Ensuring that only specific nursing providers are designated to reconcile medications
options.D: Focusing on verifying medications with a high risk of adverse effects
options.E: Requiring multiple care team members to review medications independently with the patient

explanations.A: Contacting family members may be appropriate in certain cases (eg, cognitively impaired patient). This patient is fully oriented; therefore, reconciliation should first be performed with the patient.
explanations.B: The patient's pharmacy can be contacted for additional verification; however, this should not substitute for direct conversation with the patient. Pharmacy records may not accurately reflect how the patient is actually taking medications or her concomitant use of nonprescription medications.
explanations.C: Limiting medication reconciliation to only designated nursing staff reduces the number of opportunities to catch mistakes and increases the risk of error. All nursing staff should be trained in medication reconciliation and encouraged to reconcile patient medications when appropriate.
explanations.D: Certain medications (eg, insulin, beta blockers) are considered high risk due to the potential for serious adverse effects. However, many medications that are considered low risk (including over-the-counter medications) can cause serious complications directly or indirectly by interacting with other medications. Therefore, all medications should be carefully included in reconciliation.

generalExplanation:
Errors in medication reconciliation (ie, the process of reviewing and updating a patient's medication regimen) occur frequently during transfer of care (eg, hospital admission). Errors include omitting active medications; including outdated prescriptions; and recording an incorrect dose, form, route, or frequency.

To prevent errors, multiple care team members should verify medications independently with the patient. This technique represents redundancy, a safety strategy used to reduce errors in complex, high-risk organizations (eg, health care, aviation).

Medication reconciliation should always involve direct conversation with the patient (when cognitively intact), address both prescription and nonprescription medications (including supplements), and include inspection of medication bottles if available. Other best practices for medication reconciliation include the following:

• Interprofessional review, including physicians, nurses, and pharmacists; each provider should review medications independently with the patient e Brief, updated review by the ordering physician prior to placing or renewing medication orders
educationalObjective: Errors in medication reconciliation (ie, the process of reviewing and updating the current medication regimen) occur frequently during the transfer of care. Prevention includes independent review by multiple care team members, interprofessional review (eg, physicians, nurses, pharmacists), and updated review prior to medication orders.

stem: A 24-year-old bicycle courier is brought to the emergency department after he was struck by a car. The patient was thrown approximately 6.1 m (20 ft) through the air and was initially unconscious when other eyewitnesses reached him. On arrival, blood pressure is 84/54 mm Hg, pulse is 130/min, and respirations are 28/min. Oxygen saturation is 88% on 100% oxygen via a nonrebreather mask. The patient appears extremely anxious and in respiratory distress. When he sees the trauma team preparing supplies for intubation, the patient says, "No, no tube!" However, soon afterward, the patient loses consciousness while resuscitative efforts and trauma survey examination are ongoing. Which of the following is the most appropriate course of action?

options.A: Consult the medical ethics committee emergently
options.B: Contact the next of kin and obtain surrogate consent for intubation
options.C: Do not intubate the patient and document his verbal refusal
options.D: Intubate the patient without obtaining consent
options.E: Perform tracheostomy instead of orotracheal intubation
options.F: Proceed with intubation and obtain retroactive consent after the patient recovers

explanations.A: Surrogate consent from the next of kin or the ethics committee is unnecessary to perform intubation in this emergency, life-threatening situation. In addition, delaying intubation to contact either party would likely cause harm to the patient.
explanations.B: Surrogate consent from the next of kin or the ethics committee is unnecessary to perform intubation in this emergency, life-threatening situation. In addition, delaying intubation to contact either party would likely cause harm to the patient.
explanations.E: Endotracheal intubation, rather than tracheostomy, is the standard of care (ie, acting in the patient's best interest) for obtaining a secure airway in the absence of upper airway obstruction and involves less risk (ie, do no harm) to this patient with a life-threatening condition.
explanations.F: Informed consent is unnecessary in this patient's emergency, life-threatening situation. Although the rationale for the emergency treatment will likely be discussed with the patient after he recovers, informed consent is never obtained retroactively.

generalExplanation:
Informed consent is typically required prior to performing any procedure on a patient; this respects patient autonomy, allowing patients to make educated decisions about their own health care. A main exception to the rule is when a life- saving procedure is necessary in an emergency and obtaining consent is not possible.

Informed refusal is the negative corollary of informed consent: if appropriately informed, patients with decision-making capacity can refuse life-saving treatment (eg, intubation). However, this requires that the same information be discussed with the patient as is typically discussed for informed consent, including:

• The diagnosis e The proposed procedure or treatment, along with its risks/benefits

• Alternative treatment options, along with their risks/benefits

• The risks of refusing treatment Although this patient stated, "No, no tube," he decompensated so quickly (eg, while trauma survey and resuscitative efforts were ongoing) that the discussion necessary for informed refusal could not be completed. In the absence of informed refusal, the physician should act in the patient's best interest and proceed with emergency endotracheal intubation, a life- saving procedure (Choice C).

A final consideration in this case is that, due to emotional (eg, fear) and/or physiological (eg, brain hypoperfusion) derangements resulting from trauma and/or hypovolemic shock, this patient may have temporarily lacked decision-making capacity to give informed refusal (or consent).
educationalObjective: Life-saving procedures (eg, intubation) may be performed without informed consent in emergencies, when obtaining

stem: A 44-year-old psychology professor with a history of chronic rheumatoid arthritis comes to the office for a follow-up examination. She is currently taking prednisone and infliximab, a regimen that has successfully stabilized her condition. She enjoys swimming 3 or 4 times a week, which helps with her strength and keeps her weight on target. Temperature is 37.2 C (99 F), blood pressure is 110/70 mm Hg, pulse is 78/min, and respirations are 16/min. The patient weighs 65 kg (143.3 Ib) and is 162.5 cm (5 ft 4 in) tall. Physical examination reveals no significant changes. Toward the end of the visit, the patient mentions that a family friend who suffers with chronic pain secondary to a spinal fusion has had a good response to acupuncture. She would like to try acupuncture instead of the medications she is taking currently. Which of the following is the most appropriate response to this patient's request?

options.A: Acupuncture is definitely something we can try; alternative treatments can be very beneficial.
options.B: Acupuncture should not be used as it has not demonstrated efficacy for rheumatoid arthritis.
options.C: I am concerned that your condition will worsen rapidly if you stop your medications.
options.D: I am not familiar with acupuncture but can refer you to a clinician experienced in the procedure.
options.E: Tell me more about your interest in trying acupuncture for your condition.

explanations.A: This response enthusiastically endorses the patient's request for acupuncture without first understanding what is prompting her request. In addition, it makes a general statement about the benefits of CAM that is inaccurate in her case given the lack of evidence for acupuncture in rheumatoid arthritis and the risks of discontinuing the current treatments.
explanations.B: Although studies have not demonstrated acupuncture's efficacy for rheumatoid arthritis, this response rejects the patient's suggestion outright without first exploring the reasons for her request. The risks and benefits of the proposed treatment can be discussed after the physician has gained a better understanding of the patient's perspective.
explanations.C: Warning the patient about the risks of stopping her current treatment regimen is dismissive of her request and likely to damage the physician-patient relationship. The first step is to understand why she is requesting a change in her treatment. The risks of stopping her current medications can be addressed at a later point.
explanations.D: It would be premature to refer the patient for acupuncture without first understanding the reasons behind her request.

generalExplanation:
Patients are increasingly interested in complementary and alternative medicine (CAM), and physicians must be prepared to discuss CAM modalities with them and integrate treatments that have demonstrated safety and efficacy. The initial response to a patient who requests an alternative approach is to explore the reasons for requesting a different treatment.

This patient may be dissatisfied or have concerns about the quality of current care. She may be experiencing bothersome medication side effects of which the physician is unaware. Once the patient's reasons are clarified, the physician can discuss the risks and benefits of the proposed CAM treatment in addition to suggesting modifications to the current treatment regimen that may address her concerns.
educationalObjective: The initial response to patients suggesting complementary and alternative medicine is to explore their reasons for requesting such treatment. Physicians must be prepared to discuss the risks and benefits of complementary and alternative approaches to treatment and be open to integrating modalities with proven safety and efficacy.

stem: As part of a new patient safety initiative to deliver high-value care, the director of an intensive care unit at a teaching hospital implements interprofessional team-based rounding. Daily patient rounds are conducted by a team that includes the attending physician, a pharmacist, a social worker, a nurse practitioner, and a case manager. Which of the following is most likely to promote highly effective functioning within this structure?

options.A: Ensuring that all team members have a similar understanding of desired goals
options.B: Prioritizing completion of team activities in the shortest amount of time
options.C: Promoting equal participation in patient care activities by each health discipline represented
options.D: Reducing team hierarchy and promoting overlap of roles among team members

explanations.B: Team efficiency is essential but should not be prioritized over achievement of team goals (eg, patient safety, addressing unexpected medical conditions). For example, additional time spent on rounding is sometimes necessary to improve coordination of care and prevent errors.

generalExplanation:
Teamwork promotes safety in high-risk, complex environments such as health care. Conducting rounds with interprofessional or interdisciplinary (ie, involving multiple health professions or disciplines) teams can prevent medical errors by improving communication and coordination of patient care activities.

Effective team functioning is promoted by ensuring that all members have a shared understanding of goals (eg, overall goals for hospitalization, immediate clinical priorities in patient care, planned studies or procedures). Teams with this shared understanding are significantly more effective in achieving intended outcomes (eg, comprehensive assessment of patient clinical status, completion of necessary patient care tasks). Additional characteristics of effective teams include: e Clear and unique (rather than overlapping) roles, which reduces unnecessary and potentially harmful duplication of effort (eg, multiple providers administering insulin to a patient) (Choice D) e Roles that are commensurate to each team member's skills, Knowledge, training, and experience. For example, although involvement of all interprofessional team members is needed to promote optimal patient care, some patient care goals (eg, assessment of overall clinical status or complex management decisions) require more extensive participation by members of specific disciplines (eg, nurse, physician) (Choice C) e Psychological safety (ie, concerns can be freely expressed without fear or intimidation) and absence of excessive hierarchy (ie, steep differences in authority levels between team members)
educationalObjective: Teamwork reduces error in complex health care settings. Effective teams are characterized by a shared understanding of goals, clear roles based on knowledge and skills (rather than authority), and psychological safety (ie, comfort in expressing concerns).

stem: A 37-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after his brother called the police to report aggressive and disruptive behavior. The brother is worried the patient "took something" that caused him to become violent. The patient appears intoxicated on arrival and attempts to punch several staff members. He is given intramuscular lorazepam and is admitted to the hospital under involuntary status. Temperature is 37.3 C (99.1 F), blood pressure is 138/70 mm Hg, and pulse is 96/min. Physical examination shows a 4-cm laceration on the left forearm with no active bleeding. An hour after admission, the surgical resident examines the patient and recommends wound irrigation and closure. The patient refuses the procedure and says, "I need to sleep. You can come back when wake up." Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management of this patient?

options.A: Do not perform the procedure, and reassess the patient after he awakens
options.B: Do not perform the procedure until consent is provided by the patient's brother
options.C: Do not perform the procedure until two-physician consent can be obtained
options.D: Perform the procedure because the patient lacks capacity to refuse due to drug effects
options.E: Perform the procedure due to imminent harm
options.F: Perform the procedure given involuntary admission status

explanations.B: The brother may act as a surrogate decision maker and provide consent only if it is determined that the patient lacks capacity to refuse treatment.
explanations.C: Two-physician consent is used only when a patient is incapacitated and there is no living will or surrogate available to make decisions for the patient.
explanations.D: There is insufficient information to conclude that this patient lacks capacity, and his refusal should be respected. At this point, it is reasonable to expect that the patient will be capable of participating in a more thorough informed consent discussion once he is less sedated.
explanations.E: Refusing treatment for a nonbleeding laceration would not pose a risk of imminent harm (eg, death, severe disability), and the procedure should not be performed without the patient's consent. Medical emergencies that require an urgent, lifesaving procedure may be performed without consent.

generalExplanation:
Although this patient was admitted under involuntary status due to intoxication and aggressive behavior, it cannot be assumed that he lacks capacity to consent to or refuse nonemergency medical treatment. The informed consent process must be conducted for all patients, including patients admitted involuntarily for substance intoxication or mental illness (Choice F).

Consent for a nonurgent surgical procedure or treatment must be given voluntarily, and the discussion must include an explanation of the diagnosis and discussion of the risks and benefits of both the proposed treatment and the treatment alternatives, including no treatment. Patients admitted under involuntary status have the right to refuse treatment for a non-life-threatening injury, and this patient's refusal should be respected. Because he was recently admitted for drug intoxication and subsequently received sedative medication (lorazepam), the possibility that drug/medication effects have temporarily influenced his ability or willingness to participate in an informed consent discussion should be considered. The procedure should not be performed, and the patient should be reassessed when he awakens and drug/medication effects have worn off.
educationalObjective: The informed consent process for procedures or treatment must be conducted for all patients, including those admitted involuntarily for substance intoxication or mental illness. Consent for a nonemergency surgical procedure or treatment must be voluntary.

Reasons are grouped into specific categories, including "staffing," "organization," "patients," and "scheduling." stem: A 44-year-old woman requests a same-day appointment due to poor sleep. The patient says that when she goes to bed, her "brain can't shut off" and she feels "too wired" to fall asleep. She has been spending hours playing online games and buying things from the Internet. The patient is well known to the physician and has a long history of bipolar disorder. Her medications include valproate and ziprasidone. Physical examination is normal. On mental status examination, the patient is very animated, laughs frequently, and speaks very rapidly. She has no hallucinations, and no delusions are elicited. The physician increases the patient's valproate dosage and prescribes a 1-week supply of zolpidem for sleep, with a planned follow-up in a week. At the close of the visit, the patient thanks the physician profusely and presents a gift of a sterling silver pen, saying she is so appreciative that her visit could be scheduled on such short notice. Which of the following is the most appropriate response by the physician?

options.A: "I appreciate the gift and will continue to do my best to take care of you."
options.B: "I appreciate your thanks and am happy to take care of you, but I am unable to accept the gift."
options.C: "Thank you, but I cannot accept gifts from patients unless they are inexpensive."
options.D: "Thank you, but physicians are prohibited from accepting any gifts."
options.E: "Thank you for the gift, but please understand that it does not affect the care you receive."

explanations.A: It would be inappropriate for the physician to accept a gift that may have been purchased as a consequence of hypomania.
explanations.C: There is no definite monetary value that determines the appropriateness or inappropriateness of a gift. The main issue in this case is the mental status of the patient, not the value of the gift.
explanations.D: There is no absolute prohibition on accepting gifts, and it would be inaccurate to tell the patient otherwise. However, if the physician has a personal rule not to accept gifts, this could be communicated to the patient.
explanations.E: Physicians should ensure (and communicate) that accepting gifts will not alter the patient's level of care. However, because of this patient's condition, it is not appropriate to accept the gift.

generalExplanation:
Accepting gifts from patients often raises complex issues. Although some physicians may decide to adopt a no- gift policy, others maintain that gifts of low value given with no expectation of preferential treatment are acceptable and that rejecting the gift can damage the physician-patient relationship. In the absence of absolute guidelines, most physicians make decisions on a case-by-case basis and consider multiple factors, including the cost, type, and timing of the gift; the apparent motivation behind giving it; and the nature and longevity of the physician- patient relationship. Gifts that are clearly extravagant, inappropriately intimate, or given to secure preferential treatment should not be accepted.

In this case, the primary concern is the patient's unstable mental state. She has a known diagnosis of bipolar disorder and her difficulty sleeping, racing thoughts, elevated mood, excessive online spending, and pressured speech are consistent with a hypomanic episode. The physician must consider that this patient's gift was purchased within the context of impaired judgment due to her hypomanic state. The gift should be politely declined with an expression of appreciation for the patient's thanks.
educationalObjective: Decisions about whether to accept gifts from patients include the cost, type, and timing of the gift and the motivation behind giving it. Gifts should not be accepted from patients experiencing a mood episode potentially affecting their judgment.

stem: A 65-year-old woman comes to the clinic due to markedly decreased urine output for the past 24 hours. The patient underwent coronary angiography by the physician's colleague 5 days ago and was discharged the next day in stable condition. Medical conditions include type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and coronary artery disease. Temperature is 37 C (98.6 F), blood pressure is 140/92 mm Hg, pulse is 88/min, and respirations are 14/min. Laboratory results show creatinine of 3.4 mg/dL and blood urea nitrogen of 40 mg/dL. Acute tubular necrosis secondary to the contrast used during angiography is suspected. Review of the medical chart before and after the procedure reveals that the patient did not receive adequate hydration prior to angiography. The patient is very concerned and asks why she is unable to urinate. Which of the following is the most appropriate response?

options.A: "Given your underlying health conditions, this is unfortunately an expected event that occurs occasionally after angiography."
options.B: "Let me ask your regular physician to call you and discuss what might have happened."
options.C: "The cause of your condition is unlikely to ever be known, but let's focus on what we can do now with the best possible care."
options.D: "This complication could have been prevented if your physician had given intravenous hydration prior to the procedure. Unfortunately, the physician forgot to do this."
options.E: "This may be related to your recent angiography, but I need to discuss it with your regular physician before I can give you a definitive answer."

explanations.A: AKI can be associated with administration intravenous contrast agents, and the risk may be greater in patients with diabetes mellitus. However, this only increases the importance of proper care and does not excuse a serious medical mistake.
explanations.B: This response completely evades the patient's direct question and is not appropriate. Even though the physician has not had the opportunity to discuss the patient's care with the colleague, a brief acknowledgment of the potential relationship of the procedure to the complication should be made.
explanations.C: Claiming that the cause of this patient's condition may never be known is deceptive, particularly since the sequence of events has a potentially clear explanation. The physician should discuss the basic facts of the case in a tactful but honest way.
explanations.D: Although intravenous hydration was not given prior to the procedure, additional information should be obtained from the responsible physician before determining that it was mistake; there might have been other reasons for not giving intravenous fluids. Also, patients can develop AKI following intravenous contrast even with appropriate precautionary measures.

generalExplanation: This patient likely has contrast-induced acute kidney injury (AKI), and her risk may have been unnecessarily increased due to lack of periprocedural intravenous hydration. Discussing a potential medical mistake made by a colleague can be awkward, especially when the patient or family is pressing for detailed information. Nevertheless, the physician should discuss the essential truth with the patient in a tactful and concise manner. Ideally, patient discussions regarding an adverse outcome should be conducted by the physician who had primary responsibility for the initial intervention. If the physician who performed the procedure is unavailable, a complete and detailed explanation may not be possible. Therefore, a brief and honest explanation should be provided to the patient immediately ("This may be related to your recent angiography"), with the assurance that a definitive answer will be provided once the matter has been fully discussed with the colleague. In the meantime, appropriate care and follow-up for the acute complication should be provided.
educationalObjective: Patient discussions regarding treatment complications should ideally be conducted by the physician who had primary responsibility for the initial intervention. If that physician is unavailable, a brief and honest explanation should be provided to the patient by the covering physician, with the assurance that a definitive answer will be provided once the matter has been fully discussed with the colleague.

stem: An 81-year-old woman with a history of chronic atrial fibrillation and mitral valve replacement, maintained on warfarin, is admitted to the intensive care unit due to pneumonia. The patient develops asymptomatic runs of ventricular tachycardia. A cross-covering provider, who is normally based in a different unit, pages the attending physician. The physician is performing a sterile procedure in another unit and asks a resident to communicate a verbal phone order for 20 mEq of oral potassium supplementation. The resident states the order as, "Give 20 of K now." The cross-covering provider enters the verbal order as, "Give 20 mg of vitamin K intravenously now." The patient receives the medication. The following day, her INR is subtherapeutic. Which of the following could have prevented this error?

options.A: Adding warning labels to look-alike drugs
options.B: Implementing a clinical decision support protocol
options.C: Practicing closed-loop technique
options.D: Standardizing sign-out communication
options.E: Using checklists prior to high-risk drug administration

explanations.A: Visual cues, such as warning labels, can prevent confusion between look-alike or high-risk medications (eg, clear antibiotic solution bags with similar appearance to intravenous fluids). In this case, selection of the wrong drug resulted from a miscommunicated verbal order rather than confusion between look-alike medications.
explanations.B: Clinical decision support tools prompt providers who place orders using computerized systems to consider safety-promoting actions (eg, review drug-drug interaction). These tools are unlikely to generate alerts for vitamin K (which may be appropriate corrective therapy when INR reversal is desired); furthermore, they would not prevent errors from verbal orders.
explanations.D: Checklists improve safety by standardizing high-risk processes (eg, preventing incomplete sign-out) and administration of high-risk medications (eg, administering tissue plasminogen activator to patients with suspected stroke). Checklists and standardized sign-outs would not prevent incorrect drug selection resulting from miscommunication of real-time verbal orders.
explanations.E: Checklists improve safety by standardizing high-risk processes (eg, preventing incomplete sign-out) and administration of high-risk medications (eg, administering tissue plasminogen activator to patients with suspected stroke). Checklists and standardized sign-outs would not prevent incorrect drug selection resulting from miscommunication of real-time verbal orders.

In this case, communication breakdown caused inadvertent administration of intravenous vitamin K rather than oral potassium (sometimes given empirically because electrolyte abnormalities exacerbate arrhythmias), resulting in reversal of warfarin-induced anticoagulation (ie, subtherapeutic INR level). Miscommunication risk increases with verbal orders, which lack safety checkpoints (eg, computerized alerts indicating drug interactions). Abbreviations (eg, "20 of K," instead of full dose and drug name) and indirect communication (eg, resident communication of attending's order) also increase error risk. Closed-loop communication, also known as "read-back" technique, is used by high-reliability organizations (eg, those with excellent safety records despite high risk) to minimize miscommunication. This technique is as follows:

1. Sender (eg, resident) conveys message (eg, specific potassium order) to receiver (eg, cross-covering provider).

2. Receiver repeats (reads back) the full interpreted message to sender.

3. Sender clarifies or confirms accuracy of message. Use of closed-loop communication would have identified and corrected this miscommunicated verbal order.

stem: A 51-year-old man comes to the office for a follow-up appointment. The patient was recently diagnosed with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), and his condition has deteriorated rapidly. Physical examination shows progressive muscle weakness and atrophy. The patient says, "I need to know that, when things get really bad and can't take care of myself, you will help me end my life. I haven't discussed this with my wife yet, but I think she would agree that it would be better to end my suffering when the time comes." The patient has no psychiatric history and is not currently suicidal. Which of the following is the most appropriate response to the patient's request or concern?

options.A: "I understand that this disease has affected all aspects of your life; let's focus on how we can optimize the remaining time you have with family."
options.B: "I'm concerned your mood may be changing your outlook; would you consider speaking with a counselor before making this decision?"
options.C: "Not having control of how your symptoms progress can be distressing; have you considered how ending your life would affect your family?"
options.D: "This is not an uncommon request given the progressive nature of ALS; we can discuss your decision in detail when the time comes."
options.E: "You've been thinking about the end of your life and what that might be like for you; let's talk more about how you came to this decision."

explanations.A: This response ignores the patient's request and will likely make him feel that his concerns are not being heard. It fails to explore the reasons behind the patient's request and misses the opportunity to discuss potentially beneficial palliative care interventions.
explanations.B: This response assumes that the patient is depressed and avoids having a difficult end-of-life conversation by recommending that the patient speak to another provider. The physician has an established relationship with this patient and should explore the issue with him first. If further counseling or intervention is required, a referral to a mental health specialist can be made.
explanations.C: This response is likely to elicit guilt rather than encourage exploration and understanding of the patient's experience and fears.
explanations.D: Deferring the conversation to a later date can contribute to even greater distress because the patient's concerns are likely to grow over time. Palliative care interventions to address the patient's concerns and improve quality of life should be discussed now.

generalExplanation:
Physician-assisted suicide is the process by which a physician helps competent patients voluntarily end their lives when faced with end-of-life suffering. It involves providing medication, a prescription, or information to a patient with the understanding that the patient intends to use it to complete suicide. Although it is legal in a few states and in some countries, physician-assisted suicide is a controversial area of ethics. Physician-assisted suicide should be differentiated from euthanasia, in which a physician administers a lethal substance. In the United States, euthanasia is illegal and is considered unethical.

When approached with such a request, the physician should respond with empathy and compassion and explore the reasons for the request. Reasons may include fears of loss of autonomy and dignity, fears of suffering (eg, uncontrolled pain, dyspnea) and poor quality of life, and feelings of not wanting to be a burden to others. Once the patient's fears and concerns are identified, the physician can discuss palliative care options that address these specific issues. Palliative care interventions to improve quality of life include adequate pain control, psychologic support, comfort care, and appropriate multidisciplinary referrals (eg, hospice, counseling, spiritual).
educationalObjective: The initial response to a request for physician-assisted suicide should include exploring the patient's reasons for the request. Once the patient's concerns and fears are identified, the provider can optimize palliative care interventions to address specific issues and improve quality of life.

stem: A 75-year-old-man is admitted to hospice care for end-stage multiple myeloma. He has severe pain due to pathologic vertebral compression fractures and osteolytic rib lesions. The pain remains uncontrolled despite a continuous intravenous morphine infusion; the infusion rate has been increased several times, most recently 2 days ago. Temperature is 37 C (98.6 F), blood pressure is 140/75, pulse is 95/min, and respirations are 10/min. Pulse oximetry is 89% on room air. On examination, the patient is drowsy but constantly moans in pain and opens his eyes when his name is called. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in the management of this patient?

options.A: Continue morphine at the same dosage and reevaluate in 48 hours
options.B: Decrease morphine gradually to maintain a respiratory rate of 212/min
options.C: Increase morphine until adequate pain control is achieved
options.D: Stop morphine and administer naloxone immediately

explanations.A: A dose adjustment of continuous morphine infusion may be made as early as 8 hours after the last dose adjustment (ie, time to reach steady state). This patient's current dose has reached steady state; waiting another 48 hours would prolong unnecessary suffering.
explanations.D: Although administering a reversal agent such as naloxone may be tempting due to the patient's respiratory depression and sedation, doing so would precipitate acute opioid withdrawal. This could cause needless suffering contradictory to the patient's goals of care.

generalExplanation:
This patient with end-stage malignancy has transitioned to hospice care, in which the focus shifts toward maximizing comfort (eg, pain control) versus extending length of life. He has inadequate pain control despite his current morphine dosing and has evidence of sedation and respiratory depression (eg, respirations <12/min, hypoxemia).

For patients with terminal illness (eg, advanced cancer), interventions that have adverse effects (eg, respiratory depression) are justified if they are given with the intention of promoting the patient's well-being or allowing for a comfortable death (ie, doctrine of double effect). Therefore, it is appropriate to increase this patient's morphine dose despite his sedation and respiratory status. This practice contrasts with management of chronic pain without terminal illnesses, in which serious adverse effects (eg, respiratory depression) require opioid dose reduction and pursuit of alternate pain control modalities (Choice B).
educationalObjective: Opioids are the foundation of pain relief in end-of-life care. In hospice care, in which the goal is to maximize comfort, opioids may be used to promote comfort despite the potential of hastening the dying process.

stem: The medical director of a health insurance plan is evaluating the plan's spending on health care costs of covered beneficiaries in a particular geographic region. Over the past year, the plan's highest health care costs have occurred from hospitalizations, imaging studies, and prescriptions for nongeneric medications. Beneficiaries incurring the highest health care spending were most likely to have 23 chronic disease diagnoses. Which of the following approaches is most likely to decrease the plan's spending on health care while improving the quality of health care for beneficiaries?

options.A: Limiting the covered length of hospitalizations for plan beneficiaries
options.B: Reimbursing providers whose patients achieve specific improvements in health outcomes
options.C: Requiring a trial of generic medication for all patients before a newer drug is covered
options.D: Requiring providers to obtain the plan's approval prior to ordering expensive medical services

explanations.A: Imposing broad restrictions (eg, hospitalization length, nongeneric medications) or requiring providers to obtain advance approval for higher-cost services (eg, imaging) can reduce health care spending. However, these measures have been criticized for also lowering the quality of care by delaying or restricting treatment for patients who require these services to optimally manage disease.
explanations.C: Imposing broad restrictions (eg, hospitalization length, nongeneric medications) or requiring providers to obtain advance approval for higher-cost services (eg, imaging) can reduce health care spending. However, these measures have been criticized for also lowering the quality of care by delaying or restricting treatment for patients who require these services to optimally manage disease.
explanations.D: Imposing broad restrictions (eg, hospitalization length, nongeneric medications) or requiring providers to obtain advance approval for higher-cost services (eg, imaging) can reduce health care spending. However, these measures have been criticized for also lowering the quality of care by delaying or restricting treatment for patients who require these services to optimally manage disease.

generalExplanation:
High-quality health care is characterized by timely, safe delivery of evidence-based care. High-quality care avoids resource overuse (eg, inappropriate imaging or medication use), which can lead to patient harm and worse health outcomes (eg, iatrogenic effects). Among this insurance plan's beneficiaries, the highest-cost services include hospitalizations, nongeneric medications, and imaging studies. While these services may be necessary for certain patients, possible overuse may be lowering overall quality and leading to unsustainable health care costs.

Pay-for-performance (P4P) programs can optimize resource use while improving overall quality of care. P4P offers providers additional reimbursement when patients improve in predefined health outcomes (eg, completion of cancer screening, meeting goal hemoglobin A1c). P4P encourages providers to: e Engage in resource stewardship (eg, evidence-based use of health care resources), reducing spending on unnecessary services e Deliver timely care (eg, offering cancer screening at recommended intervals)

e Promote improved health outcomes (eg, better diabetic control)

Accountable care organizations (ACOs) are an example of a health system incorporating P4P structures. An ACO brings groups of providers (eg, primary care clinicians, pharmacists, hospitalists) and healthcare facilities (eg, hospitals, nursing homes) to coordinate care, with the goal of improving quality and reducing costs. Providers receive bonus reimbursements based on the proportion of patients achieving targeted quality metrics and health outcomes.
educationalObjective: Pay-for-performance programs, which are used in accountable care organizations, link financial incentives to predefined quality metrics (eg, percentage of patients completing cancer screening). They optimize resource use (eg, avoiding unnecessary treatment) while promoting timely, evidence-based health care.

stem: A 52-year-old man undergoes emergency laparotomy for peritonitis after he was stabbed in the abdomen during a robbery. During the operation, minor spillage of enteric contents is discovered, and a small bowel injury is found and repaired. When the rest of the intraabdominal organs are examined for injury, an approximately 10 cm gastric mass is found that appears most consistent with a gastrointestinal stromal tumor. Resection of the mass would require partial gastrectomy. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Do not resect the mass because of the increased risk of infection
options.B: Do not resect the mass because of the lack of patient consent
options.C: Do not resect the mass to limit operative time in the setting of trauma
options.D: Resect the mass because of the high likelihood of malignancy
options.E: Resect the mass to avoid another operation in the setting of abdominal adhesions
options.F: Resect the mass to decrease total medical costs and recovery time for the patient

explanations.D: A gastric mass of this size (ie, 10 cm) has a high likelihood of malignancy, and resection is likely to be recommended after complete workup (eg, imaging to rule out lymph node involvement or metastases). However, it is the patient's (not the surgeon's) right to choose (or refuse) resection, even if the mass is malignant.

stem: A 27-year-old woman, gravida 2 para 1, at 39 weeks gestation comes to labor and delivery while in active labor. Her prenatal care has been uncomplicated, and her prior pregnancy ended in a spontaneous vaginal delivery of a 7-lb (3.2-kg) infant at term gestation. The patient has no chronic medical conditions, and her only medication is a daily prenatal vitamin. Prepregnancy BMI was 22 kg/m² and the patient has gained 28 Ibs (12.7 kg) during this pregnancy. The patient rapidly progresses to 10-cm cervical dilation and begins pushing. Her delivery is complicated by a shoulder dystocia lasting 3 minutes, which requires maternal hip hyperflexion, suprapubic pressure, and delivery of the posterior arm to facilitate delivery. Apgar scores are 4 and 7 at 1 and 5 minutes, respectively. The infant exhibits a brachial plexus palsy and is transferred to the neonatal intensive care unit. Which of the following is the best way to reduce complication rates for shoulder dystocia?

options.A: Conduct a debriefing for team members after each adverse event
options.B: Perform a root cause analysis after every adverse event
options.C: Schedule simulation drills with the entire clinical team at regular intervals
options.D: Use a checklist that categorizes shoulder dystocia risk in every patient chart

explanations.A: Team debriefings are interactive discussions focused on safety concerns and actions in a specific situation. They can improve team communication and coordination, but their benefit is limited to the involved teams. In contrast, all obstetric staff members require regular training for shoulder dystocia. In addition, debriefings are less effective than SBT in improving technical skills (eg, maneuvers needed for prompt resolution of dystocia).
explanations.B: Root cause analysis is a retrospective process performed after an adverse event to systematically identify all causes leading to the event. It is most useful for generating recommendations to address preventable errors. In contrast, most shoulder dystocias are unpredictable/unpreventable and require the routine practice of technical skills.
explanations.D: Checklists that categorize patients by shoulder dystocia risk based on patient characteristics (eg, BMI, diabetes mellitus) are ineffective for predicting or preventing shoulder dystocia because >50% of patients with shoulder dystocia have no identifiable risk factors, as in this patient.

generalExplanation:
This patient had a shoulder dystocia, or fetal shoulder impaction behind the pubic symphysis that impairs delivery. Shoulder dystocia is an infrequent obstetric emergency, which may result in neonatal (eg, brachial plexus injury, hypoxic encephalopathy) and maternal (eg, postpartum hemorrhage) complications. Risk factors include diabetes mellitus, fetal birth weight 24,500 g, and obesity with excessive gestational weight gain. However, shoulder dystocia is highly unpredictable (making it difficult to prevent) and can occur even when no risk factors are identified, as in this patient.

Due to the unpredictable nature of shoulder dystocia, all staff members (eg, nurses, obstetricians) require training at routine intervals to refresh clinical knowledge and technical skills. Simulation-based training (SBT) is particularly helpful because team members can train together and gain hands-on practice using simulated patient scenarios. This approach improves team performance (eg, rapid, coordinated response) and technical skills (eg, maneuvers to resolve dystocia). Scheduled SBT sessions have been associated with reduced rates of neonatal complications (eg, brachial plexus injury) from shoulder dystocia.
educationalObjective: Simulation-based training prepares teams to respond effectively and rapidly during high-risk clinical emergencies (eg, shoulder dystocia). This hands-on training can improve team performance, refine technical skills, and reduce

stem: The director of a neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) notes an elevated failed extubation rate of 47% among preterm infants. She decides to implement a quality improvement (QI) plan with the goal of reducing the failed extubation rate by 30%. The director determines that the primary issue responsible for the elevated failed extubation rate is a lack of standardized extubation strategies. She leads a team to design a new extubation checklist and standardized protocol, which form the cornerstone of the QI plan. She provides 4 training sessions over 2 weeks to the NICU physicians and staff, all of whom pass a post-test administered after the training. Based on the Plan-Do-Check-Act paradigm, which of the following is the most appropriate subsequent action?

options.A: Implement the new protocol and evaluate variations in failed extubation rates after a predetermined time
options.B: Obtain informed consent from the infants' parents for participation in a formal randomized controlled trial of the new protocol
options.C: Request institutional review board approval of the new protocol to ensure ethical care of patients
options.D: Schedule another set of training sessions now and retest staff to ensure material retention in 1 week
options.E: Send a preliminary report to hospital leadership on the failed extubation rate and describe the new protocol

explanations.B: The approach described in this case represents a QI project that does not include an experimental intervention. It does not require approval by the institutional review board (ie, research ethics board), a randomized controlled trial, or additional informed consent.
explanations.C: The approach described in this case represents a QI project that does not include an experimental intervention. It does not require approval by the institutional review board (ie, research ethics board), a randomized controlled trial, or additional informed consent.
explanations.E: Areport could be provided to hospital leadership but is not a necessary element at this junction of the cycle when results have not yet been obtained. Reports to leadership are sometimes useful in the early stages of a QI project if the project requires significant additional resources, which does not seem to be the case in this scenario.

generalExplanation:
The Plan-Do-Study-Act (PDSA) and Plan-Do-Check-Act (PDCA) paradigms are quality improvement (QI) tools that involve cyclical processes with the goal of continual improvement. Once a Ql issue is identified (eg, elevated rate of failed extubations among preterm infants), a 4-step process is put in place to address it, as follows: e Plan: Identify any factors contributing to the issue (eg, lack of standardized extubation strategies), set an objective (eg, reduce failed extubation rate by 30%), and put a plan in place to carry out a cycle (eg, new protocol and checklist development, training in preparation for implementation).

e Do: Implement the plan (ie, new protocol) while making sure to collect data and document problems and unexpected observations.

e Study (or Check): Using the data gathered, complete a data analysis that compares the results obtained to the objectives set (eg, evaluate variations in failed extubation rates). Although the terms PDSA and PDCA (which may have developed in different settings) are sometimes used interchangeably, the use of "S" ("Study") in PDSA is felt to better emphasize the need for a full analysis.

e Act: Based on these data, identify changes that need to be made and lessons learned, and then begin work on the next cycle if needed to achieve the objective.

These 4 steps can be repeated as needed. Adjustments may be considered based on results. For example, another training session may be useful to provide additional instruction or to ensure retention; however, it is unlikely to be helpful at this time given the recent training and post-test administration (Choice D).
educationalObjective: The Plan-Do-Study-Act and Plan-Do-Check-Act paradigms are quality improvement tools. They are 4-step cyclical processes with the goal of continual improvement.

stem: A 17-year-old boy is hospitalized with an acute exacerbation of cystic fibrosis. His respiratory function had remained stable for many years but has begun to deteriorate, with 3 hospital admissions within the past 6 months. The patient's FEV1/FVC ratio has decreased compared with a baseline reading taken 9 months ago and is 30% of predicted value. He is placed on supplemental oxygen, antimicrobial therapy, and inhaled bronchodilators. The hospitalist physician notices that there are no advance directives for this patient's care. Which of the following is the best approach to take?

options.A: Contact the patient's primary care doctor and recommend that a discussion take place after discharge
options.B: Defer a discussion until the patient's condition has stabilized so that he does not lose motivation to participate in treatment
options.C: Involve the patient in a discussion about treatment options and advance care directives
options.D: Obtain legal consent from the patient's parents and implement their directives as soon as possible
options.E: Wait until the patient turns age 18 and is able to provide legal consent for his own directives

explanations.A: Aprimary care clinician who knows the patient well is in the ideal position to initiate a discussion about advance care planning. However, given this patient's deteriorating clinical status, it is inappropriate to defer the conversation until after discharge (in case he develops a significant respiratory decompensation during this hospitalization) or until the patient turns age 18 (the age of legal consent in most jurisdictions).
explanations.E: Aprimary care clinician who knows the patient well is in the ideal position to initiate a discussion about advance care planning. However, given this patient's deteriorating clinical status, it is inappropriate to defer the conversation until after discharge (in case he develops a significant respiratory decompensation during this hospitalization) or until the patient turns age 18 (the age of legal consent in most jurisdictions).
explanations.B: It is inappropriate to defer the conversation based on the assumption that the patient would lose motivation to participate in treatment. Studies have found that adolescent patients and their families are able to tolerate a wide range of emotions during the advance care planning conversation and find the experience to be beneficial.
explanations.D: Adolescents can understand medical implications and are likely to find it demeaning to be left out of conversations about their end-of-life wishes. Excluding this patient from the discussion and relying solely on the parents' directives would be inappropriate.

generalExplanation:
This patient with cystic fibrosis (CF) has experienced an increased frequency of pulmonary exacerbations and a decrease in FEV1. These findings correlate with decreased survival and therefore warrant timely discussion about advance care planning. It is important that adolescents with a chronic and life-limiting illness, such as CF, be provided the opportunity to participate in these discussions.

Studies have found that a family-centered approach involving the adolescent is effective and helpful. Discussions should include information regarding prognosis and care options, including detailed information about lung transplantation and the patient's and family's preferences for end-of-life care. Gaining an understanding of the patient's priorities and values ensures that the patient's wishes are respected should a life-threatening complication occur during hospitalization.
educationalObjective: Discussions regarding advance care planning for adolescents with chronic, life-limiting illnesses (eg, cystic fibrosis) should take a family-centered approach and directly involve the adolescent patient. Discussion should include information regarding prognosis, care options, and the patient's and family's preferences for end-of-life care.

stem: A 43-year-old Viethamese-speaking woman comes to a busy primary care clinic due to back pain. She is accompanied by her 14-year-old son, who speaks English. The physician does not speak Vietnamese. He uses a videoconference system to reach a certified Vietnamese interpreter, who then translates the physician's words into Vietnamese and the patient's words into English. The physician diagnoses the patient with lumbosacral back strain, prescribes a 15-day course of naproxen, and counsels the patient on how to use the medication. Which of the following actions by the physician is most likely to result in the patient using the medication as counseled?

explanations.C: When patients are competent and independent, directly engaging the patient is preferred over relying on family members, especially in this case where the patient's son is a minor.
